blocks.x: COM SKILLS 157 · Communication Skills · Topic 5

Every piece of effective writing and speech is built out of sentences — and every sentence can be classified in two independent ways: by how it is structured (how many clauses it has, and how they relate) and by what it does (state, question, command, or exclaim). This topic gives you both systems of classification, with the exact test sentences you'll be expected to recognise and produce.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Explain what a sentence is — a group of words expressing a complete thought, made up of a subject and a predicate.
2Describe the four structural sentence types — simple, compound, complex and compound-complex — and their structural distinctions in terms of independent and dependent clauses.
3Distinguish between simple, compound and complex sentences using real example sentences, and correctly turn a pair of related simple sentences into a complex sentence.
4Distinguish between declarative, interrogative, imperative and exclamatory sentences by their grammatical structure ([SV(O)(C)(A)], [VS(O)(C)(A)], [V(O)(C)(A)]) and punctuation.

5Use the appropriate sentence form to convey different communicative functions — recognising, for example, that a declarative sentence can be used to ask a question, and an interrogative sentence can be used to give a command.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Sentence A group of words which expresses a complete thought. A sentence has two main components — a subject (who or what the sentence is about) and a predicate (what is said about the subject, built around a finite verb). For example: Kofi (subject) is my friend (predicate).

Two systems of classification Sentences are classified along two separate axes that you must not confuse: their structure (how many independent and dependent clauses they contain — simple, compound, complex, compound-complex) and their function (what communicative job they do — declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory). Any structural type can, in principle, be used to perform any function.
Subject + Predicate→ Structural Types (clause count)→ Functional Types (communicative purpose)→ Accurate, Varied Writing
Classifying by clause structure

Sentences are grouped into four main types according to their structure — specifically, according to how many independent clauses and dependent clauses they contain, and how those clauses are joined together.
The Simple Sentence

Simple sentence Consists of a single independent clause. It contains one main idea, and has a subject and a finite verb. The students always go church. The director of the company walked into the office.

Simple sentence with a compound subject A simple sentence may still have more than one subject joined by and or or — it remains simple as long as there is only one clause (one subject-predicate unit acting together). The houses and the cars were damaged. The teacher or his student pays for the book.
The Compound Sentence

Compound sentence Consists of two or more independent clauses joined by a comma, a semicolon, or a coordinating conjunction such as and, or, nor, or but. Each clause could stand alone as its own sentence — they are simply linked together as equals. John bought the book and (he) paid for it. Kofi played the drum but Ama didn't dance. He neither swept the compound nor washed the car.
The Complex Sentence

Complex sentence Has one independent clause and one or more dependent (subordinate) clauses. The dependent clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence — it depends on the main clause for its full meaning. It may begin with a relative pronoun (when, who, where) or a subordinating conjunction (until, so that, because, since, while), and might tell us when something happened, which person was involved, or where the event took place. When he came, we had already eaten. Since you are the father, give him some advice.
Building a complex sentence

You can build a complex sentence out of two simple sentences by turning one of them into a dependent (subordinate) clause. For example: English is not our mother tongue. + English has gradually become the most important language in Ghana. → Although English is not our mother tongue, it has gradually become the most important language in Ghana.
The Compound-Complex Sentence

Compound-complex sentence As the name suggests, contains two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses combined in the same sentence — the "compound" part comes from the linked independent clauses, and the "complex" part comes from the added dependent clause(s). Kofi played his drum this morning but Ama didn't dance because Charles was not there. (two independent clauses — Kofi played his drum this morning and Ama didn't dance — joined by but, plus the dependent clause because Charles was not there.) Students have cleaned up the beaches, and they have planted flowers in the parks so that the shores will look inviting to visitors.
Quick comparison of the four structural types

c: John bought the book and paid for it.
When he came, we had already eaten.
Kofi played his drum this morning but Ama didn't dance because Charles was not there.

blocks.title: Practice: spotting the four types in running text

items: Read a passage sentence by sentence and count the clauses: is there one subject-verb unit that can stand alone (simple), two or more linked as equals (compound), one main clause plus a subordinate one introduced by a word like which, because, or although (complex), or a mixture of both patterns in one sentence (compound-complex)?

A sentence such as "...but every time she took a step, she might have fallen over her shoe lace, which dragged from unlaced shoe" combines an independent clause with subordinate clauses introduced by every time and which — a compound-complex structure.

Watch for coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, nor) signalling compound structure, versus subordinating conjunctions/relative pronouns (because, when, since, while, who, which, where) signalling complex structure.

blocks.x: Classifying by communicative function

Functional classification asks what a sentence does rather than how many clauses it has. Declarative sentences make statements; interrogative sentences ask questions — but each can, in the right context, be pressed into service for other communicative purposes too.
The Declarative Sentence

Declarative sentence A sentence that makes a statement or a declaration. It is a proposition that expresses an opinion, a fact, or a judgment. A statement may be true or false, positive or negative. Mondays follows Sunday. (True) Two and two is/are three. (False) Kwame likes Alice. (Positive) Kwame dislikes Alice. (Negative)
Structure of the declarative sentence

items: 1Basic pattern: SV(O)(C)(A). Declarative sentences have a subject followed by a verb, optionally followed by an object, complement and/or adjunct. The boy snores noisily. (SVA) · The girl is clever. (SVC)

2Declarative sentences may have no visible subject. Good to see you. (understood: It's good to see you.) · Serves you right. · John bought the wallet and (he) paid for it. — the repeated subject is dropped.

3A verb may precede the subject when a negative adverbial is front-shifted. Some adverbs with negative meaning (scarcely, hardly, barely, rarely, seldom) can be moved to the front of the sentence. When they are, they trigger subject-verb inversion, and the auxiliary do is often inserted to keep the sentence grammatical.

blocks.x: Fronted negative adverbials & inversion I scarcely visit my hometown these days. → Scarcely do I visit my hometown these days. (correct — auxiliary do inserted and inverted before the subject) *Scarcely I visit my hometown these days. (ungrammatical — no inversion) I can hardly imagine what to say. → Hardly can I imagine what to say. Other adverbials that trigger this inversion when fronted: He barely entered his car when the robbers attacked → Barely had he entered his car when the robbers attacked. · My brothers rarely quarrel → Rarely do my brothers quarrel. · My sister seldom accommodates visitors → Seldom does my sister accommodate visitors.
Other functions of declarative sentences
Although declarative sentences are grammatically statements, they are routinely used to perform other communicative acts, depending on context, tone and situation.
To ask a question
You have paid your fees? — a statement form used, with rising intonation, to ask.
To make a request
I would love a cup of tea. — phrased as a statement of desire, functioning as a polite request.
To give a command
You will leave the room now! — a statement about the future used to issue an order.
To express prohibition
You can't go out now. — a statement of inability/permission used to forbid.
To express emotion
God save the king! — a declarative form used to voice strong feeling.
To make a suggestion
You could be cooking. — a statement of possibility functioning as a suggestion.
To give a warning
That dog is dangerous. — a plain statement of fact that also warns the listener.
The Interrogative Sentence

Interrogative sentence A sentence that asks a question. Interrogative sentences may demand answers. How old are you? · When did you arrive? · Have you eaten? · Your father has come? (a declarative form used interrogatively, with rising intonation)

Structure of the interrogative: VS(O)(C)(A) Interrogative sentences place a verb before the subject. The verb that comes before the subject is always an auxiliary verb (Will she come?). In writing, interrogatives end with a question mark. In speech, a yes/no question ends in rising intonation, while a wh-question ends in falling intonation.
Types of interrogatives
Yes/No questions

Questions that demand yes or no for an answer, e.g. Are you tired? They are formed from statements by placing the auxiliary verb before the subject: You have eaten. (statement) → Have you eaten? (question).
Wh-questions

Formed with a wh-word — who, what, which, whose, when, where, why, how — and demand a piece of information as an answer, e.g. Who won the prize? · What is your name? · When did you come? · How old are you?
The "dummy do" in yes/no questions

Dummy do Where a statement has no auxiliary verb, the auxiliary do must be introduced to carry the inflection (tense/agreement) of the main verb, before the subject-verb inversion happens. Ama sells rice. (statement) → *Ama do sell rice. (introduction of "dummy do") → Ama does sell rice ("does" matches the singular subject) → Does Ama sell rice? (question, do inverted before subject) Ama sold rice. (statement) → *Ama do sold rice. (dummy do) → Ama did sell rice ("did" matches the past tense) → Did Ama sell rice? (question)
Practice: turning statements into yes/no questions
The student attended lectures last week. → Did the student attend lectures last week? Monday comes before Tuesday. → Does Monday come before Tuesday?
Other functions of interrogative sentences
To make an assertion
Isn't it Abu who is praising me? — a rhetorical question really asserting that it is Abu.
To give a command
What are you looking at on your phone? — phrased as a question, functioning as an order to stop.
To give an invitation
Won't you have a glass of beer? — a question used to politely invite.
To insult
Can't you think? — a question form used to belittle or insult.
To make a request
Would you read through the script for me, please? — a polite request phrased as a question.
To express emotion
Isn't Ellen a beauty? — a rhetorical question used to express admiration.

items: Declarative: SV(O)(C)(A) — subject comes before the verb; ends with a full stop; states, but can also question, request, command, prohibit, express emotion, suggest, or warn depending on context.

Interrogative: VS(O)(C)(A) — an auxiliary verb comes before the subject; ends with a question mark; asks, but can also assert, command, invite, insult, request, or express emotion depending on context.
Both types share the same underlying idea: form and function are not always the same thing — the grammatical shape of a sentence does not always match the communicative job it is doing.

blocks.x: Commands and outbursts
The last two functional types complete the set: imperative sentences give commands and directions, while exclamatory sentences express surprise, emotion, or strong feeling.
The Imperative Sentence
Imperative sentence A sentence that gives a command. Imperative sentences are used when giving a direct command, directions, instructions, or orders. Stand up. · Sit down. · Go straight.
Structure of the imperative sentence

Structure: V(O)(C)(A) It is the base form of the verb which begins the sentence, optionally followed by an object, complement and/or adjunct. Sit down. (VA) · Close the door. (VO) · Be a man. (VC) · Close the door immediately. (VOA)
Types of imperative sentence
Second person imperative
There is no overt (visible) subject — the imperative verb begins the sentence directly, and the subject "you" is implied. Keep off the grass. = (You) keep off the grass.
First and third person imperative
Introduced by the word "Let" placed before the subject. First person: Let us keep off the grass. · Let me rest for today. Third person: Let them pay their dues. · Let them come.
Other functions of imperative sentences
To make a wish
Have a nice week-end. — imperative form used to wish someone well.
To give an invitation
Let's share a cup of tea. — a "Let" imperative used to invite.
To give a warning
Mind your language. — a command used to caution.
To make a threat
Laugh again or I punish you. — a command-plus-consequence used to threaten.
To make a prohibition
Don't go out in that dress. — a negative imperative used to forbid.
The Exclamatory Sentence

Exclamatory sentence A sentence that expresses surprise, emotion, or feeling. Exclamatory sentences end in an exclamation mark. What a fantastic goal! · Aren't these girls beautiful! · You are fantastic!
Note

Notice that Aren't these girls beautiful! has the inverted VS structure normally associated with an interrogative, but because it ends in an exclamation mark and expresses admiration rather than seeking an answer, it functions exclamatorily rather than interrogatively — a further reminder that structure and function are separate systems.
The four functional types at a glance

items: Let them come. → imperative (third person, introduced by "Let").
You have paid your fees? → declarative structure (SV) used to ask a question.
What a fantastic goal! → exclamatory, expressing surprise/admiration, ends in "!".
Would you read through the script for me, please? → interrogative structure (VS) used to make a polite request.
